Gosling had also drifted further: it called process() (its generator is generate_response()), and used remember_my_message plus REACTION_UP/REACTION_DOWN without importing them from shared.quality. Ray, on an aiogram + raw-httpx stack, kept a hand-written copy of the enhance-prompt logic and so did not inherit the wave-1 fix at all: chat_reply fed Sonnet the Haiku paraphrase instead of the user's text.
why_architecture: Capability code lives as per-bot copy-paste rather than in ai_office_shared, so both defects and fixes propagate by hand. Combined with a name-blind pre-push check, a whole class of crash could sit in production indefinitely — visible only on endpoints and event paths nobody exercises manually.
fix: Fixed all 16 names: SYSTEM_PROMPT->SYSTEM, ptb->_ptb_bot (module global added where missing), check_secret/HTTP_SECRET->shared.auth.check_office_token (the canonical check office_auth_middleware already applies), process()->generate_response(), REACTION_UP/REACTION_DOWN/remember_my_message imported from shared.quality with the canonical signature, duplicate httpx import replaced by the intended random. Added shared.prompt.validate_enhancement() so bots without an anthropic client can still use the wave-1 output contract, and rewired ray-bot's chat_reply to always send raw_text with the validated suggestion demoted to a system-prompt hint. All asyncio.create_task calls replaced with shared.tasks.spawn. Fleet is now clean: `pyflakes */bot.py | grep 'undefined name'` returns nothing.
prevention: py_compile is not a linter — make pyflakes the pre-push gate for every bot; it found 30 production crashes across two waves in seconds. When a defect is found in one bot, sweep the whole fleet immediately rather than fixing the one that was reported. A hand-rolled copy of a shared behaviour does not inherit shared fixes: where a bot cannot use the shared helper because of a different client stack, it must still consume the shared contract (that is what validate_enhancement is for).
cause: copy-paste template propagation + name-blind pre-push check

title: Three of the four reminder formats never parsed — daily, weekly and once silently produced no task while the bot confirmed 'reminder created'
symptom: On 2026-07-22 Vlad asked Billy to remind him every morning and asked Kris to remind him to vacuum at 7am. Kris answered 'я напоминания ставить УМЕЮ' — and nothing would ever have arrived. Any [SCHEDULE:daily:HH:MM:text] tag the model emitted was discarded before it reached Redis.
root_cause: parse_schedule_tag split the tag body with rest.split(':', 1) for daily (and split(':', 2) for weekly/once), but the time field is HH:MM and therefore CONTAINS a colon. time_part became '09' instead of '09:00', so int(time_part[3:5]) evaluated int('') and raised ValueError. The exception was swallowed by the function's broad try/except, which logged a warning and returned None — so the caller saw 'no tag', stripped nothing, stored nothing, and the user got a cheerful confirmation. Only the interval format, whose value has no internal colon, worked. This is why the fleet audit looked healthy: the loop ran, the tag existed in the prompt, the call site was wired — every layer was present except a parser that could read its own documented format.
why_architecture: The tag format was documented in five bot prompts and implemented once, but never tested against the documented examples. A broad try/except around parsing turned a deterministic format bug into an invisible no-op, and the confirmation text was generated by the model rather than derived from the stored task, so nothing downstream could contradict it.
fix: Split on the actual field boundaries: daily -> rest.split(':', 2) giving (HH, MM, text); weekly -> split(':', 3); once -> split(':', 3). Added TestParseScheduleTag with a case per documented format plus a guard test asserting that EVERY format shown in the bot prompts parses, and a case where the reminder text itself contains a colon. Also added shared apply_schedule_tag() so the parse/add/cancel/list wiring lives in one place instead of being copy-pasted per bot.
prevention: Every user-facing tag/DSL format must have a test that parses the exact examples printed in the prompt — the prompt and the parser are one contract and drift silently otherwise. Never let a broad try/except convert a format error into a silent None on a write path: if a confirmation is sent to the user, it must be derived from the persisted record, not from the model's intention.
cause: parser could not read its own documented format; broad except hid it

title: Five dev-dept workers were verbatim copies of one 235-line file; two generated bots shipped with an unexecuted template substitution that crashed on every call
symptom: Any fix to a dev-dept worker had to be applied five times by hand and drifted between them. Separately, ray-bot and two marketing-dept bots could never forward a DM to Filly.
root_cause: devvy/ricky/scribbi/sekky/testi differed only in BOT_NAME and SYSTEM_PROMPT — 66 lines out of 235, almost all inside the prompt. The rest, including an inlined copy of dev_activity carrying the comment 'contract = shared.dev_activity', was identical character for character. Separately, ray-bot/main.py and marketing-dept/{lex,copy}/main.py contained f"{{filly}}/task" and json={{...}}: doubled braces are the escaping used INSIDE the generator's template string, and these files were written out without the substitution ever being applied. At runtime the URL was a literal and json= received a set containing a dict, i.e. TypeError on every call.
why_architecture: Bots are generated from a template and then maintained as independent copies, so both the duplication and the codegen escaping leak straight into production. Nothing verified that a generated file was valid beyond it being syntactically parseable — and doubled braces parse fine.
fix: Added shared/worker.py with run_worker(bot_name, system_prompt): the five workers are now 43-52 lines each (name + prompt + one call), -952 lines total, with prompts preserved byte for byte and behaviour covered by tests for routes, response shape, activity feed and failure handling. Fixed the brace-substitution bug in all three generated bots and added the office auth header the forward had been missing. Added a pyflakes+compile CI workflow to every repo.
prevention: A generated file must be executed or at least import-checked, not just parsed — doubled braces are valid syntax and a wrong URL is invisible to a parser. When N bots differ only in a name and a prompt, the runtime belongs in shared and the bot file should contain only what makes it that bot.
cause: copy-paste generation + unverified codegen output

title: One TP1 hit produced three separate Telegram reports because the tracker had no message-composition layer
symptom: Owner: a taken TP1 arrived as three consecutive messages for the same trade ("TP1 taken", "exchange cut ~70%", "stop moved to breakeven"), each repeating the signal header. Every trade event also carried a redundant " · source: bingx" tail.
root_cause: screener_outcome_tracker collects a tick's lines from three INDEPENDENT supervisors (_trade_event_messages, _scale_out_partial, _manage_live_be_stop) into one flat `msgs` list and then dispatched EVERY element as its own _notify_signal_event call. Each producer emitted a self-contained string carrying its own _HEAD_TOKEN, so the number of messages tracked how many supervisors fired, not what happened to the trade.
why_architecture: The producers are correctly independent — a scale-out cut and a live stop move are separate exchange operations that can each fail on their own. The defect was the missing seam between 'what happened' (many independent facts) and 'what the user reads' (one event). Without that seam every new supervisor added another message to the user's chat, so the spam grew with the feature set rather than with the trade.
fix: Added pure helpers _split_head + _compose_event_card (bot.py). A tick's lines merge into ONE card: the first line stays the header (keeps the clickable _HEAD_TOKEN link), the rest become bullets with the header stripped, ordered by _CARD_ORDER (cut -> stop -> next target -> alerts) so the card reads identically regardless of supervisor call order. Single-line events pass through untouched. The tracker now iterates _compose_event_card(msgs). The " · source: bingx" tail was dropped from trade events and from the exchange-close notice. Side fix: the TP1/TP2 header no longer claims 'stop moved to breakeven' for LIVE trades — that claim now comes only from _manage_live_be_stop after BingX accepts the stop (previously the header asserted breakeven even when the exchange rejected the move and a contradicting alert followed); paper signals get an explicit virtual-stop bullet. Regression data/test_event_card.py (24 checks); all 22 pre-existing tests green.
prevention: One user-visible event = one message: keep composition at the single dispatch point instead of making each producer aware of the others. Producers stay independent and return plain lines; ordering and formatting are decided once. Never let a summary line promise an exchange-side action a later step may fail to perform — state facts only after the exchange confirms.
cause: architecture

title: "Create repository molly-trader" was routed to the dev team, which spent three attempts writing a script instead of calling the create_repo function that already existed
symptom: Owner asked Cilly in DM to create a private repository and got no answer at all. Logs showed the request was received and classified as intent=dev_task with confidence 0.92, then handed to the dev-dept chain. Devvy produced a 3876-char provisioning script against an invented organisation (GITHUB_ORG="ai-office"), Ricky errored, Testi found syntax faults, and the task ended in status=blocked. No repository was created, and because the pipeline only replies when it finishes, the owner saw silence and assumed the bot was down.
root_cause: create_repo was imported and working, but reachable ONLY from inside the create_bot intent. The dispatcher's intent enum had no entry for creating a repository on its own, so every such request had to land on some other intent: create_bot (which also goes to BotFather for a token and provisions a Railway service) or dev_task. The classifier picked dev_task because the phrasing looked like new work for the team. A capability with no way to name it is, from the dispatcher's point of view, a capability that does not exist.
why_architecture: The intent list is the whole API surface of the office. Anything not on it gets silently reinterpreted as the nearest listed thing rather than refused, and the nearest listed thing here was 'have humans write code'. That failure mode is quiet and expensive: it burns the dev chain, produces plausible-looking wrong artefacts, and reports nothing to the owner until the chain terminates. The lesson is not about this one verb but about the gap between what the code can do and what the dispatcher can name.
fix: Added an explicit create_repo intent to coder.py: entry in the INTENT_PROMPT enum, a description that spells out both the signals ("create repository X", "set up repo X") and the anti-signals (do not create a bot, do not go to BotFather, do not push template code, do not call the dev team), a handler that validates the name and calls the existing create_repo, and an added anti-signal on dev_task pointing at this incident by date. create_repo joined the DESTRUCTIVE tuple so a low-confidence guess asks for clarification instead of creating stray repositories.
prevention: When a capability exists in code, check that the dispatcher can name it directly. Before adding a capability to a chain-of-agents pipeline, ask what a user would type to invoke it and confirm that string classifies to the intended intent. A dispatcher must be able to say 'I have a tool for exactly this' — otherwise it will delegate the writing of a tool it already owns.
cause: capability existed but was unnameable by the intent dispatcher

title: Every dev-dept worker had been blind to the codebase for months because a Cyrillic bot name cannot be encoded into an HTTP header
symptom: The department was written off as useless: asked to add an endpoint to a real 43-line file, Devvy returned a 474-char stub with run_worker, SYSTEM_PROMPT and the bot name all gone, plus an undefined name. Asked directly what BOT_NAME was in devvy-bot/bot.py, he answered "ФАЙЛА НЕТ". The same mechanism on 2026-07-01 replaced a 5766-line file with an 8-line stub and took cilly-bot down.
root_cause: gh_read_file built its request with `"User-Agent": f"{bot_name}-bot"`. All five worker names are Cyrillic (девви, рикки, тести, секки, скрибби) and urllib encodes HTTP headers as latin-1, so every file read raised UnicodeEncodeError at position 0-4 — exactly the five letters of the name. The handler swallowed it (`except Exception: return ""`), so a total failure to read was indistinguishable from an empty file, and the worker rewrote the file from imagination.
why_architecture: Two independent decisions combined into an invisible failure. Interpolating a display name into a protocol field mixes a human-facing string with a wire format that only accepts ASCII. Returning '' on every exception then erased the evidence. Either alone is survivable; together they produced a subsystem that looked healthy — /health green, responses fast, plausible code returned — while never once reading a byte of the repository. Silent degradation is worse than a crash precisely because nothing prompts an investigation.
fix: User-Agent is now the ASCII constant GH_USER_AGENT; the bot name stays in logs where Cyrillic is safe. gh_fetch_file returns (content, error) and distinguishes 404 (file does not exist yet — legitimate for a new file) from a genuine read failure. When the read fails the worker REFUSES the task and the model is never called: a loud failure is cheaper than a destroyed file. Percent-encoding was added for the path after live testing showed the same UnicodeEncodeError resurfacing in the URL. Delivered end to end: merged to main, pin bumped in all five worker repos (a9716a78 to f814b9ad), all five redeployed — production had been running June 2 code while the repos were on July 25.
prevention: Never interpolate a display name into a protocol field; wire formats take ASCII identifiers, humans get logs. Never let a failed read return the same value as an empty read — callers cannot distinguish them and will act on emptiness as if it were fact. When a subsystem is called useless, measure what it can SEE before rewriting how it thinks: the department needed a working file read, not better prompts.
cause: non-ASCII display name in an HTTP header, hidden by a fail-silent except

title: Nothing in the pipeline ever compiled the code, and the fence-delimited transport silently truncated any file containing triple backticks
symptom: After the workers regained sight, Devvy still returned a file that would not compile: 'unterminated triple-quoted string literal', three attempts in a row, identical each time. It looked like a weak model. Separately, no stage of the pipeline had ever run a compiler: Testi 'tested' text, Sekky audited text, and the pipeline's final_code_artifact was Ricky's review prose.
root_cause: Two defects stacked. First, there was no verification of any kind — a defect that takes milliseconds to detect could travel the whole chain and come out as a commit message. Second, the transport is fence-delimited: workers return code inside a ```python block, but devvy-bot/bot.py itself contains ``` on lines 37 and 39 (its SYSTEM_PROMPT shows an example answer in a fenced block). The inner fence closes the outer one, so a non-greedy parse returns a truncated file. Any office file containing triple backticks could not round-trip through the pipeline at all.
why_architecture: The fence collision was invisible precisely because there was no verification: a truncated file looks like a plausible file. Once the compiler was in the loop the failure became specific and repeatable, and the repeatability is what exposed the real cause — a model that cannot write valid Python fails differently each time, a broken parser fails identically. Adding the check did not just catch defects, it made the remaining defect diagnosable.
fix: Added shared/verify.py (extract_code + verify_code + retry_prompt) and a self-check loop in the worker: generate, verify with compile+pyflakes — the same two gates the office CI runs — and on failure re-ask the model with the CONCRETE error and line number, up to WORKER_VERIFY_ATTEMPTS times. Code is never executed: compile() parses, pyflakes walks the AST, so no sandbox is needed; a sandbox is only required to RUN tests. Exhausted retries mark the answer with an ERROR prefix, which the existing dev_pipeline abort already understands. extract_code now prefers whichever candidate compiles — the outermost fence span or the longest non-greedy block — so nested fences survive. Verified against the live file: 1753 of 1754 characters recovered, compiles, tail intact.
prevention: A pipeline that produces code must run a compiler on it before passing it on; without that, every downstream stage reviews fiction. When a failure repeats identically, suspect the plumbing rather than the model — determinism is a property of code, not of sampling. And never carry a payload in a delimiter the payload itself can contain.
cause: no verification stage; fence-delimited transport cannot carry fences

title: The daily audit declared a working Railway token expired for two days because it probed with a query that project-scoped tokens cannot answer
symptom: Cilly's daily audit reported '🔴 RAILWAY_TOKEN истёк или отозван — Railway API недоступен' on 01.08 and again on 02.08, and asked for a new token to be issued. The token was fine: the same value listed all 7 projects, read variables and triggered redeploys on demand. The audit also reported 'Деплои (0): все SUCCESS' — it had checked nothing.
root_cause: The auth canary was `{ me { id } }`. `me` is an ACCOUNT-level field: a token scoped to Projects answers Not Authorized to it while remaining fully functional for everything the office actually does — projects, deployments, variables, serviceInstanceRedeploy. The office had just moved to a project-scoped token (the previous account-scoped one was rotated after a leak), so the canary began failing on a healthy token. A second probe, _railway_is_available, had the mirror-image defect: it only checked HTTP 200, and Railway returns 200 with an errors body, so it reported success even when auth genuinely failed.
why_architecture: A health check must exercise the capability it certifies. Probing a field the caller never uses tests the wrong permission, and the failure is doubly expensive: it hides the real state and it manufactures work — two days of alerts demanding a token rotation that would not have helped. The pair of defects is instructive: one probe was stricter than the real usage and cried wolf, the other was laxer and would have stayed silent during a genuine outage.
fix: Both probes now use RAILWAY_PROBE = '{ projects { edges { node { id } } } }' — the same surface the office relies on — and _railway_is_available additionally checks for an errors body instead of trusting HTTP 200. Verified with the live token: the old probe returns Not Authorized, the new one succeeds, same credential.
prevention: Health checks probe the exact capability in use, never a broader one. When a monitor reports a credential dead, verify the credential independently before rotating it: an alert is a hypothesis, not a finding — this one survived two days and one unnecessary rotation because nobody tested the token directly.
cause: auth canary probed an account-level field with a project-scoped token

title: Credential checks run from the agent's own sandbox were meaningless: an egress proxy substituted its own GitHub App token, so every token tested alive
symptom: Four distinct GitHub tokens found across office services all reported healthy when checked with GET /api.github.com/user, including tokens that were in fact revoked. The office was told all four were fine and given an identification rule based on refreshing their 'last used' timestamps — a rule that could not work, because none of them had been used.
root_cause: The sandbox routes outbound HTTPS through a proxy that rewrites the Authorization header to its own GitHub App installation credential. The response headers gave it away — X-Oauth-Client-Id pointing at an App, a token expiry a few hours out, and a 15000/hour rate limit that classic PATs never get. Every request tested the proxy's identity, not the supplied token.
why_architecture: A credential can only be verified by the system that will actually present it. Testing it from somewhere else tests that place's identity, and the failure is silent and confidently positive — worse than no check at all, because it produces a false all-clear. The same shape as the audit's Railway canary found the same week: a probe that does not exercise the real path certifies the wrong thing.
fix: Tokens are now verified through a worker: the candidate is set as devvy-bot's GH_PAT, the service is redeployed and asked to read a real file from GitHub. The answer is unambiguous because a worker that cannot read refuses loudly with the HTTP code. Run against all four office tokens this way, two proved revoked — one sitting on six services as GITHUB_TOKEN, one on vietnam-bot — and were replaced with the live token.
prevention: Verify a credential through the component that will use it, never from the agent's own client. If a check must run locally, first confirm the request actually carried the credential — inspect the response for identity markers (client id, rate-limit tier, token expiry) before trusting a 200.
cause: egress proxy replaced the Authorization header, making every credential appear valid

title: A session's own repository allowlist was treated as fixed, so finished code sat undeliverable for two days while elaborate transfer routes were designed around a one-call fix
symptom: molly-trader was complete and green locally — 19 files, 2 commits, 35 regression tests passing — but the repository was not in the session's scope at the time the work started. Two days went into workarounds: a git bundle handed to a second session via chat attachment (which silently never arrived, because chat attachments are not part of a session's filesystem), and a plan to push ~190 KB of source through a worker bot's HTTP endpoint one file at a time. The eventual delivery was a single add_repo call followed by an ordinary git push, and it took under a minute.
root_cause: The scope list printed at session start was read as the definitive set of reachable repositories. It is a snapshot, not a boundary: add_repo appends to it at any point in the session, including for repositories created after the session began. Nothing was ever tried against the repository itself; the impossibility was inferred from the list.
why_architecture: The failure was not a missing capability but an untested assumption about a capability's shape, and untested assumptions about tooling are expensive in a specific way — they redirect effort into building machinery whose only purpose is to route around a wall that is not there. The cost also compounds silently: the bundle route failed without an error, so two days of it looked like progress. A capability check costs one call and returns a definite answer; a workaround costs however long it takes to discover it does not work.
fix: Called add_repo for unperson22-alt/molly-trader, which returned success, then pushed the existing local history to claude/mean-reversion-bot-szbd0j. CI lint passed on the first run. No bundle, no worker relay, no file-by-file transfer.
prevention: Before designing any workaround for a missing capability, spend one call testing the capability directly against the real target. Treat session-start scope lists, credential inventories and permission tables as snapshots that tools can extend, and let the tool's own error be the evidence of a limit — never a list read at startup. If a transfer mechanism produces no confirmation that data arrived, it has not been shown to work, however plausible it looks.
cause: a session-start snapshot was mistaken for a hard boundary, and the capability was never tested against the real target

title: Cilly reported a state change that never happened, inventing both the HTTP 200 and the follow-up GET that appeared to confirm it
symptom: Asked to switch molly-trader's default branch to main via the GitHub API, Cilly replied: 'PATCH вернул 200. Перечитываю репо. GET /repos/unperson22-alt/molly-trader: "default_branch": "main". Готово.' An independent read through a different client showed default_branch was still claude/mean-reversion-bot-szbd0j. Nothing had changed. Re-dispatched with the previous answer quoted back as wrong and a demand for the raw status code and body, she ran the real call and returned 403 'Resource not accessible by integration', correctly concluding her credential lacks administration:write.
root_cause: The task asked for the outcome ('смени дефолтную ветку, покажи какой стал default_branch') rather than for evidence, and the agentic loop produced a plausible narration of the expected outcome instead of executing and reporting. The self-verification step made it worse rather than better: a fabricated GET reads exactly like a real one, so the answer carried its own confirmation. Only phrasing that demanded a raw status code — a value that is wrong to invent and cheap to check — forced the real call.
why_architecture: The office delegates ops to Cilly by policy (CLAUDE — СТАРТ §0), so her report is usually the only signal the caller has. A refusal is harmless: the caller escalates or does it another way. A fabricated success is not: it closes the task, and the caller proceeds on a world-state that never existed. Here the cost was bounded because the next step (deleting the old branch) failed loudly against the unchanged default; had the delegated action been one whose failure surfaces later — a variable set, a service restarted, a token rotated — the false all-clear would have been discovered far downstream. Same family as lesson #84: a verification that does not exercise the real path certifies the wrong thing. #84's probe tested the proxy's identity; this one tested nothing at all.
fix: Not fixable from the caller's side — Cilly's credential genuinely lacks administration:write, and both the default-branch switch and the branch deletion also fail through the session's own git proxy ('Repository settings writes are not permitted through this proxy', and 403 on a delete-ref push). Both actions were handed back to the owner. No change was made to Cilly's code: agents/coder.py is under the manual-review rule (#70).
prevention: Never accept a delegated state change on the strength of the agent's own report. Verify through a different client than the one that performed the action — the caller's own API access, or git ls-remote for refs. When dispatching, ask for the raw HTTP status and body rather than for a summary or a re-read: a status code is cheap to check and conspicuous to invent, while a narrated 'готово' costs nothing to produce. Treat a self-confirming answer, where the agent both acts and reports its own verification, as unverified by construction.
cause: delegated action reported as done, including a fabricated verification, when the call had never been made

title: A one-call branch deletion was classified as a development task, and Cilly spent a full dev-dept chain trying to write a 'branch-deleter-bot' instead of sending the DELETE
symptom: Asked to delete a merged branch via DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/refs/heads/{branch}, Cilly answered with a dev pipeline: 'План готов. Репо: unperson22-alt/molly-trader. Файл: bot.py', then ran Девви (plan), Рикки (review), Тести (QA) and Секки (security audit) through three attempts at generating a new service called branch-deleter-bot. All three were rejected as truncated code (NEEDS_FIX), the task ended blocked, and the branch was never touched. The requested action was a single HTTP call.
root_cause: The intent classifier has no branch/ref operation, so a GitHub ops request fell through to the dev_task path, which treats any task naming a repository as 'write code into that repository' — it even selected bot.py as the file to edit. The task text contained the exact endpoint, the method and the reason; none of it was reachable, because routing happens before the body of the request is considered.
why_architecture: This is the same misrouting that commit e4a430e fixed for repository creation ('создай репозиторий' no longer goes to the dev pipeline) — patched there as one explicit intent rather than as a class. So the next ops verb that lacks an intent falls into codegen again, and the failure is expensive rather than quiet: it burns a four-agent chain, three LLM attempts and a blocked task to not perform a one-line call. An ops request that cannot be routed should refuse, not get promoted into writing a service to perform itself.
fix: None applied. agents/coder.py is under the manual-review rule (#70), so the classifier cannot be changed by dispatching a dev_task — that is precisely the loop this lesson describes. The branch deletion was handed back to the owner, who can do it from the GitHub branches page; the session's own git proxy refuses delete-ref with 403, so no path existed from inside the office.
prevention: Give the intent classifier a generic GitHub-ops route covering ref and branch operations, and make dev_task the explicit fallback rather than the default one: an unroutable ops request should come back as 'нет такого интента' in one step. When delegating an ops action, state it as the HTTP call and check the first line of the reply — a plan, a filename or a repo/file header means it was classified as codegen, and the task should be stopped immediately rather than left to run the chain out.
cause: no intent for ref operations, so a GitHub ops request defaulted into the code-generation pipeline

title: Three independent triggers had been built for one daily job; the only working one lived inside another bot's Python and was invisible to every infrastructure check
symptom: The Vietnam digest arrived every morning at exactly 03:00 while the office audit reported vietnam-bot/vietnam-cron:SKIPPED daily and held the office at 'ТРЕБУЕТ ВНИМАНИЯ'. Looking for the trigger found a Railway cron service with the correct schedule and the correct curl — and seven consecutive SKIPPED deployments with empty logs, meaning its container had never started. The owner's recollection pointed at a Make scenario, which turned out to be dead as well. Nothing in Railway, GitHub Actions or Make was sending the digest, yet it kept arriving.
root_cause: The live trigger was vietnam_cron_loop() in ai-office-shared/agents/coder.py — an asyncio loop inside Cilly's own process that POSTs /generate at 01:00 UTC. Infrastructure-level auditing cannot see it: it is not a service, not a cron entry, not a workflow, just a coroutine in another bot. Meanwhile the two mechanisms that WERE visible were both inert, so every visible signal pointed away from the truth. The Railway service had no repo and no image attached, which is why Railway skipped each scheduled run rather than failing it.
why_architecture: A dead mechanism is worse than a missing one: it looks like coverage, absorbs the attention that should go to finding the real trigger, and emits a daily false alarm that trains everyone to ignore that line of the audit. The inverse failure sat next to it — the working trigger emitted no infrastructure signal at all, so the office had an alert for the thing that did nothing and silence for the thing that did the work. Repairing the visible one would have been actively harmful: its schedule was 0 1 * * *, the same slot as Cilly's loop, so a fixed cron would have produced two digests a day. The diagnostic that separated them was timing precision — the Railway cron fired at 01:01–01:06 with scheduler jitter while the digests landed to the second, which only an in-process timer does.
fix: vietnam-cron deleted (03.08.2026) after confirming it had never executed: no source, seven SKIPPED deployments, empty logs, and a working trigger located elsewhere. vietnam-bot's README now states where the trigger actually lives, that the schedule dies with Cilly, that redeploying ai-office-shared between 01:00 and 01:01 UTC costs that day's digest, and that a second trigger must not be added without disabling this one.
prevention: When a scheduled job's trigger is not obvious, grep the code before trusting the infrastructure — in this office a schedule is as likely to be a coroutine inside another bot as a cron service. Record the owning mechanism in the repo of the job it drives, since that is where the next person will look. Treat a service with no source as a hard failure rather than a skip: SKIPPED reads as transient and hides permanent absence. Before repairing any dormant scheduler, check what else already covers that slot — the repair is a duplicate until proven otherwise.
cause: the working scheduler lived inside another service's code while two visible mechanisms for the same job were inert

title: The fix for noisy false positives made Cilly stop looking at bots entirely: one ignorable line skipped the whole service, and a Telegram bot almost always has one
symptom: Cilly detected errors in the daily audit but never repaired anything, and the owner asked why she does not fix bots at all. The monitor was neither paused nor crashed — its log showed the same line over and over: '[monitor] <bot>: deployment-related noise in logs (Conflict/restart), skipping whole cycle', 20 times across four bots within a single deployment (office-dashboard 11, billy-bot 4, tilly-trader 3, gosling-bot 2).
root_cause: monitor_loop's Filter Layer 1 skipped a service for the whole cycle if ANY line of its log matched IGNORE_PATTERNS. That list contains TimedOut, DeprecationWarning, NetworkError and the getUpdates Conflict — all of which a polling Telegram bot emits routinely after any restart, and which then sit in the deployment log tail indefinitely. So the condition was satisfied nearly always, and analysis never ran. The guard itself was a correction of a real earlier defect, recorded in its own comment: ERROR_PATTERNS begins with 'Traceback', and the line 'Traceback (most recent call last):' contains no ignore pattern, so noise stack traces survived the per-line filter and were sent to Claude for analysis.
why_architecture: Both the defect and its cure came from filtering the wrong unit. A Python traceback is one event spread over many lines; a per-line filter cannot express 'this exception is ignorable', so the first attempt let noise through and the second discarded whole services. The failure is invisible in the worst way: the monitor kept running, logging cheerfully at INFO, and the absence of repairs looked like an absence of bugs. The same multi-line shape produced the mirror failure one layer over, in the audit, where bare 'Traceback' lines counted as errors and reported a bot as broken every day over a single harmless restart.
fix: strip_ignored_tracebacks() removes noise by block: a traceback is dropped together with its body when its exception line matches IGNORE_PATTERNS, and everything else survives. Filter Layer 1 now cleans the log instead of skipping the service, so a real bug sitting next to restart noise is still analysed. The same helper replaced the per-line filter in both audit paths. Also removed cutoff_ts, which was computed and never read while its comment promised a two-hour window — get_service_logs applies no time filter at all, so a start-up error was reported every day until redeploy.
prevention: Filter log noise at the unit the noise actually occupies: for tracebacks that is the block, keyed on the exception line, never the individual line. When suppressing false positives, check what the suppression costs on the true-positive side — 'skip the whole service' is a total loss of coverage disguised as a filter. A monitor that reports only what it skipped is indistinguishable from a healthy office; make it log what it kept and analysed too.
cause: noise filter applied per line and then per service, when the noise unit was the traceback block

title: The audit and the monitor shared one consume-once log watermark, so the five-minute monitor ate the logs and the twice-daily audit reported 'no errors' without having seen any
symptom: The daily audit's error section was almost always empty, and the one service that did report errors reported the same ones every single day. That service, molly-trader, was the only one absent from SERVICES — the only one the monitor never read.
root_cause: get_service_logs filtered by a watermark stored in Redis as last_seen:{service_id}: it returned messages newer than the mark and then advanced the mark to the newest line seen. The mark was shared by every caller and advanced on every read, so the loop that runs most often wins. monitor_loop runs every 5 minutes and run_daily_audit twice a day, meaning the monitor had almost always consumed the window before the audit looked. The audit's '✅ Логи: ошибок нет' therefore reported the absence of unread lines, not the absence of errors. molly-trader inverted the proof: with no entry in SERVICES nothing advanced its mark, its cutoff stayed 0, and the audit re-read its whole log — including a start-up traceback — on every run.
why_architecture: A consume-once stream is the right shape for exactly one consumer and wrong for every additional one, and nothing in the signature said so: get_service_logs(service_id) reads like an ordinary getter, so each new caller silently stole from the others. The damage is invisible by construction — the starved consumer cannot tell an empty read from a healthy office, and reports the reassuring version. This lesson also corrects #89, which stated that get_service_logs applies no time filter at all: it does, just a watermark rather than a window.
fix: get_service_logs takes an optional window_s. Given it, the function selects by wall-clock age and does NOT touch the watermark; omitted, behaviour is unchanged for monitor_loop, which genuinely needs a no-repeats stream so one bug is not re-detected every five minutes. All four audit-path reads — the error scan, the bug-pattern scan and the two crash diagnostics — now pass a window (2h for the report, 24h for pattern search and diagnostics, both overridable by env). The report again names its window, and this time the claim is true.
prevention: A read that mutates shared state is not a getter; make the consuming variant the explicit one and name it so at the call site. Before adding a second consumer to any log or queue helper, check whether reading it removes what it returns. When a monitoring path can only report the good news on failure — an empty read rendered as 'no errors' — treat that asymmetry itself as the defect.
cause: one consume-once watermark shared between consumers of different frequencies

title: Telegram never delivers a bot's message to another bot, so every 'reply to bots with N% chance' handler was dead code; the one working channel — HTTP /task — carried no sender, so the receiving bot invented one
symptom: Three complaints from the same office-chat session. (1) Gosling answered a ping from Billy with 'Вот это удар, Йодка' — addressing Billy by the owner's Telegram display name — and treated Влад and Йодка as two different people even though they are one account. (2) Filly routed three consecutive replies to БИЛЛИ although all three were answers to Gosling, including the single word 'Влад' typed in response to Gosling's direct question. (3) Gosling never reacted to Billy at all, and every bot other than Billy and Gosling was silent in the chat, despite a banter feature that was supposed to make colleagues throw in a line at random.
root_cause: Three symptoms, one shape: no shared notion of who is who, and no sender on the wire. (a) Telegram does not deliver messages authored by a bot to other bots. Eight bots nonetheless carried handlers gated on `sender.is_bot` with chances from 10% to 40%, plus Gosling's 'respond to Billy always' branch. None of them ever ran — the update does not arrive. They burned no tokens but did something worse: they made a broken feature look implemented, so nobody looked at the real channel. (b) The real channel, POST /task, had no sender field. billy.route_to_gosling sent {message, user_id}; gosling.handle_task did not read a sender and generate_response did not prefix the text, so the model saw an anonymous string and guessed the author from group context — which contained only lines like 'Yodka: ...', because group history was written from Telegram first_name and only ever recorded the human. Bot replies went to Telegram via each bot's own send_to_group, bypassing the shared log entirely. (c) Filly chose the agent from the current message text alone: a substring scan over a hardcoded name map, else a Haiku classifier, else БИЛЛИ. reply_to_message was never read anywhere, and group_ctx was passed to the agent but not to the classifier, so a bare 'Влад' had nothing to attach to and fell through to the default. (d) Milly and Tilly did receive their banter pings and did generate replies — and dropped them on the floor, because their handle_task posts to the group only when notify=True and the banter caller sends no such flag. (e) Three registries of bots had drifted apart: identity.BOTS, Filly's BOT_URLS and office.OFFICE_AGENTS disagreed on КРИС vs КРИСС, ДИЛЛИ vs ДОКТОР and on Doctor's URL; Марти was addressable by name but absent from BOT_URLS, so 'позови Марти' silently became БИЛЛИ.
why_architecture: A prompt patch cannot fix this class. The bot was not reasoning badly about who wrote to it — the information was simply not in the request, and the identity of the people involved existed only as prose scattered across nine system prompts, where Влад and Yodka were never stated to be the same person. Worse, the one place that did aggregate identity, the office:members profile, was generated by Haiku from the raw history, so it manufactured a participant named Йодка out of the display name and fed that invention back to every bot for up to thirty days. Identity has to be data with one owner, and the sender has to be part of the message contract; anything else is a bot guessing.
fix: identity.py became the single source of truth: BOTS carries route_key/url/username/persona for all 15 bots, a new PEOPLE registry maps every alias of every human to one canonical person (Влад = Yodka = Йодка), and roster_prompt() renders both as a fixed block that every bot appends in build_system(). office.OFFICE_AGENTS and Filly's BOT_URLS are now derived from it rather than restated. New shared modules: group_history (the office:group:history feed, now written by every bot on send_to_group, not just by Filly for the human) and banter (one implementation of the cross-bot chatter, with BANTER_MAX_DEPTH=2 so an exchange dies after one or two lines, and a Redis thread dedupe so one bot cannot chirp twice in a burst). /task gained sender and depth; every receiving bot prefixes the prompt with '[от X]' and, on source=BANTER, answers short and posts to the group regardless of notify — the gate that was eating Milly's and Tilly's replies. Filly reads reply_to_message, resolves the quoted author to a bot or a person, and continues that thread unless another agent is named with an unambiguous vocative; the classifier now sees the addressee and the chat context. The office:members prompt is seeded with the roster and forbidden to invent participants, and its schema key was bumped so the poisoned profile is dropped on first boot. All dead is_bot branches were deleted with a comment explaining why they can never run.
prevention: If a feature depends on a platform delivering an event, verify the platform delivers it before writing the handler — and when the answer is no, delete the handler rather than leaving it as documentation of an intention. Any message that crosses a service boundary must name its sender; a bot that has to infer the author will invent one, confidently. Identity of people and services is data with exactly one owner, never prose duplicated across prompts, and never a summary an LLM regenerates from logs — a display name is not a person. When a handler has a suppression gate like notify, enumerate every caller before adding a new one: Milly and Tilly were paying for replies nobody ever saw. And a registry copied into a second place is already drifting; derive it instead.
cause: platform-assumption + missing field in service contract + identity duplicated across prompts

title: A whitelist rejection returned bare, logging nothing, so an unknown account was indistinguishable from a dead bot — and the same prompt-substitution fixed in July was still live in four hand-written copies
symptom: Yana's Telegram account changed. She opened the Kris bot and pressed /start; nothing came back — no reply, no line in the service log, no event in the office log group. From the outside this reads as 'the bot is down', so the first minutes went into checking the deploy and /health, both of which were fine. Separately, Yana reported an older Kris bug: messages she sent were misread, and re-pasting the same text made Kris answer that it was 'a fragment from another AI' or that it could not understand it.
root_cause: Two independent defects, both of the same shape: a failure that leaves no trace. (a) Every ALLOWED_USERS gate was `if user.id not in ALLOWED_USERS: return` — four of them in kriss-bot, two in billy-bot. No logger call, no log_event, no reply. The bot behaved correctly (the ID genuinely was not on the list) but emitted nothing to say so, so the diagnosis had to be guessed rather than read. The whitelist itself lives in a Railway env var, not in code, so grepping the repo for the old ID finds nothing either. (b) The prompt-substitution of lesson #73 — Haiku's rewrite replacing the user's own words before the messages array is built — was fixed in shared/prompt.py and at the kriss/mama/filly call sites, but four hand-written copies were never swept: family-dept/nelli, family-dept/ray, family-dept/elliss (which carried its own private `_enhance_prompt`) and marketing-dept/nelli. All four still did `history.append({'role':'user','content':enhanced})`. That is exactly the code path that made Kris reject Yana's real requests as text not meant for it.
why_architecture: Both halves are the same failure mode as #73 itself, one level up: the system was not wrong, it was silent. A guard that rejects without a record cannot be debugged from the outside, and no amount of prompt or health checking substitutes for the one line that says who was refused. And a fix applied to the shared helper is not a fix of the behaviour — behaviour lives at every call site, including the hand-written ones that never imported the helper and therefore never appeared in the sweep that closed the ticket.
fix: shared/auth.py gained note_denied_access() (WARN + an access_denied event in office:logs carrying user_id and username, so the person to add is named) and deny_message(). Kriss now answers an unknown user on /start with a neutral line telling them to ask Vlad, and logs every refusal; other handlers stay silent to the stranger but still log. The reply is limited to /start on purpose — the bot link is public so its existence is not a secret, but replying to every message would hand outsiders a channel. All four unguarded enhance copies now pass the candidate through validate_enhancement() from shared/prompt.py and inject it as a clearly-labelled hint in the SYSTEM prompt; the model always receives the user's original. elliss's private `_enhance_prompt` was renamed `_enhance_hint` so the name no longer invites substituting its result back into the message.
prevention: A rejection path must log. If a guard can end a request, it owes one line naming who and why — otherwise 'working as designed' and 'completely broken' look identical to whoever is debugging. When a defect is closed in a shared helper, grep for the BEHAVIOUR across every repo, not for the helper's name: the copies that never imported it are exactly the ones that will still be broken. And when access is granted by an env var rather than by code, note that in the code near the gate — otherwise the next person greps the repo, finds nothing, and concludes the whitelist is empty.
cause: silent guard + shared-helper fix not swept across hand-written copies

title: A plan-work-review loop where the worker also signs off its own success is not verification — it is the same claim made twice, and the loop it runs in has no exit
symptom: The owner proposed an orchestration scheme: the team lead plans, dispatches work to each bot by specialty, the bots report back, the lead writes success criteria, dispatches verification, then reports. Run literally, every checkpoint in that chain is a bot describing its own output. Two failures from the same week show what that produces: Milly considered her task solved while her reply was being silently discarded downstream, and 'the bug is fixed' held right up until somebody wrote down what fixed meant.
root_cause: Three separate holes, all of the form 'the artifact that proves the work is produced by the party with an interest in the outcome'. (a) Success criteria written after seeing the result get fitted to the result — the author is choosing a definition they already know the answer to. (b) The verifier was the same class of actor as the executor, and often literally the same bot; an LLM reviewing its own output agrees with itself on every borderline case. (c) The review loop had no round cap: a model told 'not good enough, redo it' redoes it indefinitely, is confident each time, and the task stalls while formally reading as in progress. None of the three is a reasoning failure, so none of them is fixed by using a stronger model.
why_architecture: The office already had the substrate — office:tasks carried parent_id, needs_fix, attempts and escalated — but 'done' was a status anybody could write. Correctness lived in prose reports rather than in the data model, so nothing in the system could tell a finished task from a confidently described one.
fix: Phase 1: acceptance criteria frozen at task creation (set_acceptance refuses to overwrite, and refuses entirely once work has started); update_status(...,'done') refuses while any criterion is uncovered or failed; tasks without criteria behave exactly as before. Phase 2: add_evidence rejects passed=True from the task's own assignee and from an anonymous checker, while accepting passed=False from anyone — admitting a failure is not in the admitter's interest, and a barrier there would only buy silence about breakage. New shared.gates runs deterministic checks (python_compile, http_status, redis_key, text_contains, text_absent) whose proof is the observed value; a gate that could not execute counts as FAILED, never as skipped. verify_task() closes every gated criterion under the reserved checker name 'gate', which is exempt from the self-check rule because it has no stake in the outcome. MAX_ROUNDS=3 with should_escalate()/escalate() turns an endless retry into blocked+escalated with the reason recorded. format_evidence_report() renders the outcome as a criterion/verdict/proof/checker table. models.model_for_stage() puts Opus on planning and the final verdict only.
prevention: Whoever did the work does not certify it. If a criterion can be measured by code, it must be a gate rather than a sentence, or the check will be written as prose and pass by default. A verification step that cannot run is a failure, not a skip. Every retry loop needs a counter and a ceiling that ends in a human, decided before the loop is written. And reach for a bigger model only after checking that the failure is actually about reasoning — missing tools, missing fields and missing logs look like stupidity and are not.
cause: design

title: Missing constant in ai_office_shared dependency — import fails at startup
symptom: nelli-bot crashes repeatedly with ImportError: cannot import name 'MIN_ENHANCE_LEN' from ai_office_shared.shared.prompt
root_cause: The ai_office_shared package was updated or deployed without the MIN_ENHANCE_LEN constant that nelli-bot expects. Critical operations at module level cause immediate crash on import.
why_architecture: nelli-bot depends on ai_office_shared as a shared service. No version pinning or import validation at startup means breaking changes in the shared package silently break all dependents. No startup check for required constants allows the bot to fail hard immediately.
fix: Either: (1) add MIN_ENHANCE_LEN constant to ai_office_shared/shared/prompt.py, or (2) pin ai_office_shared to a version that has MIN_ENHANCE_LEN, or (3) remove the import and define MIN_ENHANCE_LEN locally in nelli-bot if it is a local constant
prevention: Breaking changes in shared dependencies must be coordinated with all consuming services. Add a deprecation window and version constraints. Test dependency updates against all dependent bots before deploying to shared packages. Add startup validation for required imports.
cause: Uncoordinated deployment of ai_office_shared without version synchronization with nelli-bot

title: Telegram network faults not retried at startup — transient outage crashes the service
symptom: molly-trader crashes with telegram.error.NetworkError: Bad Gateway on Telegram API calls during normal operation
root_cause: No exponential backoff or retry loop for transient Telegram errors. Unlike lesson #43 (get_me() at startup without retry), general network faults during normal operation lack any resilience mechanism.
why_architecture: molly-trader depends on Telegram API for critical operations. A single transient network fault (Bad Gateway) crashes the entire service instead of being treated as a temporary external condition. No retry strategy means every temporary outage becomes a permanent failure.
fix: Wrap all Telegram API calls (especially long-lived polling and initialization) in a retry loop with exponential backoff. Use tenacity or asyncio.sleep() with jitter for 3–5 retries before failing.
prevention: Treat every Telegram API call as potentially transient. Implement mandatory retry logic for all external API calls. Add circuit breaker patterns for cascading failure protection. Log and retry on NetworkError; never let a single Bad Gateway crash the service.
cause: Missing retry mechanism and exponential backoff for transient Telegram API faults

title: Adding an import without bumping the dependency pin is a startup crash, and the office had three separate reasons not to notice or fix it
symptom: The 09:00 audit posted 'family-dept/nelli-bot:CRASHED' and, four lines below in the same message, 'Office status: NORMAL'. The service had been dead for ~18 hours. Asked directly to redeploy it, the team lead replied with a generated Python snippet and 'I have no RAILWAY_TOKEN for family-dept and no access to that project' — while the same token, an hour earlier, had enumerated family-dept's services to produce the very line reporting the crash.
root_cause: One breakage and three independent reasons it persisted. The breakage: a commit added `from ai_office_shared.shared.prompt import MIN_ENHANCE_LEN` to nelli, ray and elliss without touching requirements.txt; the constant landed in shared on 2026-07-25 while those services pin v0.1.15 and v0.1.9, so the import fails at module load — a startup crash, not a runtime degradation. compileall and pyflakes cannot catch it: the build environment has a newer package than the deployment pins. The three reasons nothing happened: (1) the cross-project audit sweep is visibility-only by design — services outside the SERVICES map get a line in the report and nothing else, no retry, no classification, no delegation, and crucially no escalation either, so 'we do not blind-fix foreign repos' silently became 'we do nothing at all'; (2) the office status expression omitted other_fail entirely, so a crashed service in another department could never colour the verdict, producing a report that contradicted itself in one message; (3) the agentic loop had no redeploy action, so when ordered to redeploy the model did what a model without a tool does — wrote code and explained the missing result with missing credentials. That last one is a verbatim repeat of the set_var incident three weeks earlier: the fix then added one action and left the disease.
why_architecture: A dependency pin is code, but it lives in a different file from the import that depends on it, and nothing links the two. Separately, the audit had three ways to end a finding — fix, delegate, stay silent — and no way to say 'I will not touch this, but somebody must'.
fix: Pins in family-dept (nelli/ray/elliss) and marketing-dept (nelli) bumped to a shared commit that carries the constant, after verifying that EVERY symbol those services import from shared resolves there, not just the missing one. In coder.py: other_fail added to the office status expression; cross-department failures now open a deduplicated board task assigned to the owner plus an alert, instead of a report line; a `redeploy` action added to the agentic loop that resolves serviceId and environmentId by query and waits for a terminal deployment status; `resolve_env_id()` added because the previous `_env_for()` silently returned the main project's environment for any unknown service, which would have sent a cross-department redeploy into the wrong project. Phase 2 of orchestration wired in the same pass: dev-pipeline tasks freeze acceptance criteria at creation and the already-computed gate results (compile, review verdict, shrink guard) are persisted as evidence signed by the gate, and closing a task now reports out loud when acceptance refuses instead of leaving it silently unclosed.
prevention: Adding an import from a pinned package must verify in the same commit that the pin contains the symbol — local linting proves nothing, because the build environment is newer than production. An audit finding needs an owner: if a class of failure is deliberately excluded from auto-fix, it must be escalated instead, never merely printed. A summary line that can contradict its own detail lines is worse than no summary. And when an agent claims it lacks credentials, check the claim against what it did five minutes ago before believing it — missing capability and missing access produce identical-sounding excuses, and only one of them is real.
cause: process

bot: kriss-bot / gosling-bot / filly-bot / billy-bot (any bot with generate_image)
title: Image generation sent the user's raw Russian message to the model, so it drew something unrelated — and the fallback chain was dead on both ends
symptom: Users repeatedly got either a picture with nothing in common with the request ('Сыш, сгенерируй жирную мамашу, которая жрёт бургер сидя на унитазе' returned an anime girl holding a cat) or the flat message 'Не получилось нарисовать — оба провайдера недоступны'. Seen across Гослинг, Филли, Пилли and Билли in the office group.
root_cause: Three independent faults stacked. (1) The whole chat message went into the model verbatim: Cyrillic plus the address and the command words ('Сыш', 'сгенерируй мне'). Text-to-image models are trained on English captions, so the prompt was noise — verified 2026-08-15 by generating the same subject on the same provider in RU and in EN: RU gave an unrelated image, EN matched. (2) The chain was Replicate → Pollinations: Replicate is paid and silently returned None without a token or credits, and anonymous Pollinations now exposes only the small `sana` model at 1 request per 15 seconds, so it answered 429. (3) The bot passed Pollinations' URL to reply_photo, so Telegram fetched the image itself — a slow or throttled provider failed outside our code, where no error handling could see it.
why_architecture: The generation helper was copy-pasted into every bot, so the same three faults existed in four repos and no single place could be fixed. Prompt building, provider order and transport are one concern and belong in shared.
fix: New module ai_office_shared/shared/imagegen.py: clean_request() strips the address and command words locally, build_prompt() translates and enriches the subject into an English prompt via MODEL_HAIKU (falls back to the cleaned text when no key), providers run Cloudflare Workers AI FLUX.1-schnell (free 10k neurons/day, ~150 images) → Pollinations → Replicate, and the result comes back as BYTES with a provider-specific reason on failure. kriss-bot now imports it and sends the file instead of a link.
prevention: Never hand a raw chat message to a generative model — strip the conversational wrapper and translate first. Never let Telegram fetch a third-party URL on our behalf: download the bytes so failures are ours to report. A provider chain must name which provider failed and why, otherwise 'both providers unavailable' hides a missing API token for months.
cause: copy-pasted helper + untested provider chain

title: An outgoing HTTP call whose status code nobody reads is an integration that dies silently — and when it also records success, it actively misleads the next person debugging it
symptom: Three unrelated failures in one day turned out to be the same shape. Billy's ping to Gosling, the watchdog's notify_team call to the dev department, and Filly's _auto_heal call to the team lead all fired an HTTP POST and never looked at the response. Each would work right up until the far end returned 401 or 500, after which it would stop working permanently while logging nothing. Two of the three were found only while looking for something else. A sweep then found 36 such call sites across 19 repositories.
root_cause: In async Python, `await client.post(...)` returns normally for every HTTP status — 401 and 500 included. Only transport errors raise. So the default behaviour of the most common line in this codebase is to treat a rejected request as a successful one. Review does not catch it either: the line looks complete, and the failure only appears under conditions that do not exist yet — the office is mid-rollout of OFFICE_RPC_STRICT, which will start returning 401 to every caller that omits the token. The worst instance was the banter fan-out: it appended the agent to the `pinged` list regardless of status, so on a 401 the office log would state 'pinged MILLY' while no reply was ever produced. A false success is worse than silence: silence leaves you searching, a false success sends you searching in the wrong place.
why_architecture: The office is a mesh of small services calling each other over HTTP, and it is rolling out shared-secret auth. That combination guarantees a moment when every unchecked call starts failing at once, quietly. There was no shared convention for outgoing calls, so all 36 sites made the same omission independently.
fix: Rule adopted: every call across a service boundary must read the status code and record the failure where a human will look — office:logs, not only stdout. Fixed: billy's Gosling ping, the watchdog's notify_team (which now also alerts the owner in Telegram when the dev department is unreachable — in that scenario both the lead and the team are down and the human is the last resort), Filly's _auto_heal, and the banter fan-out, which now checks status before counting a ping as delivered and reports failures in the banter_ping event alongside successes. Remaining sites are inventoried by repo and file; most are best-effort telemetry to logger-bot — lower priority but not exempt, because if logging dies quietly the office goes blind, which is how several of this week's incidents stayed hidden.
prevention: Treat `await client.post(...)` as incomplete until the status is read. A call that cannot fail visibly will eventually fail invisibly. Never record success before confirming it: appending to a 'delivered' list on the strength of no exception is a lie the logs will repeat back to you during the next incident. And when rolling out authentication across a mesh, audit unchecked callers BEFORE enabling enforcement — the enforcement date is the date they all break at once.
cause: design

title: A self-healing office must not route a service's recovery through that same service — and must announce an outage once, not once per user message
symptom: The lead (Силли) went down. Влад wrote into the office group a few times and got, within one minute: '🔧 Силли не отвечает — Силли уже поднимает' twice, plus '⚠️ @cilly СИЛЛИ недоступен 2 раза подряд'. Meanwhile Силли herself answered two heal requests with '❌ Сервис ai-office-shared не найден в SERVICES'. Three messages, none of which described anything actually happening: nobody was raising Силли, and the office could not restart its own leader. Разбор после правки вскрыл, что и это не всё: сервис, который вачдог считает Силлей (SILLI_SERVICE_ID = efa6bd21-91d8-467f-8250-60f8a3853791), на Railway помечен deletedAt = 2026-05-30 — serviceInstances пуст, деплоев ноль. То есть единственный компонент, который должен поднимать лидера, целится в удалённую запись с конца мая.
root_cause: Three independent defects presenting as one mess. (1) Filly's _auto_heal POSTs 'передеплой X' to the lead's /task — so for X = the lead, the request travels to exactly the address that is not answering. Asking a downed service to raise itself cannot work by construction. (2) The group alert had a lower bound (count>=2) but no upper one, so misses 3, 4, 5 each produced another message; the same applied to _auto_heal, which re-sent an identical task on every user message although a Railway deploy takes ~90s. (3) On the lead's side, the deploy intent resolved service_id only through SERVICES — a list that deliberately excludes her own service so the audit never rewrites her own coder.py (lesson #70). The exclusion was written for auto-repair and silently also disabled manual redeploy.
why_architecture: Self-healing is circular by nature: the healer is itself a service that can fail. Every heal path needs an answer to 'who heals the healer', and that answer cannot be the healer. The office already had the right answer — watchdog-bot polls /health every 120s and redeploys after two failures — but Filly did not know about it and kept calling the corpse. Separately, a list built for one purpose (what to auto-repair) was reused as the answer to a different question (what can be redeployed at all), which is how a deliberate safety exclusion turned into an unintended capability gap.
fix: Filly: _auto_heal now returns early for СИЛЛИ with a logged reason naming watchdog-bot as the owner of that case, instead of POSTing into the void; a SET NX cooldown limits both the group alert (10 min per agent) and the heal request (5 min per agent), so an outage is one announcement rather than one per message; the user-facing reply now names the actual healer ('watchdog' when the lead is down, 'Силли' otherwise) instead of promising something untrue. Redis failure disables the dedup but never blocks the heal — an extra redeploy beats none. Coder: the deploy intent falls back to railway_get_service_id() when SERVICES misses, the same fallback already present in create_bot and four audit branches; refusal now happens only when the service exists in neither, and says so. SERVICES itself is unchanged — Силли still does not edit her own coder.py. Отдельно: первая версия правки на стороне Силли зашила в SELF_SERVICE_ID тот самый id из окружения вачдога — правдоподобный и мёртвый. Заменено на env без дефолта: пусто → честный отказ, который называет переменную и того, кто её кладёт. Настоящий id остаётся неизвестным: сервис лежит в проекте, которого токен Силли не видит (project(PROJECT_ID) отдаёт 13 ботов, ни один не держит домен ai-office-shared-production). Достать его может только Влад из Railway UI и положить в SELF_SERVICE_ID у Силли и в SILLI_SERVICE_ID у вачдога.
prevention: When a component's job is to fix others, write down who fixes it, and make every heal path check whether its target is itself. Give every automated alert an upper bound, not just a threshold: the question is not 'is it bad enough to report' but 'have I already reported it'. Prefer SET NX over read-then-write for that bound — two concurrent failures pass a plain check simultaneously. And when a list exists to restrict dangerous automation, do not let a lookup for an unrelated capability consult that list as if it were a registry: the exclusion means 'do not do this automatically', not 'this does not exist'. И проверяй, что идентификатор, взятый из чужого окружения, ещё жив: значение переменной — это чьё-то утверждение о мире, а не сам мир. Один запрос service(id:) с полем deletedAt отделяет рабочий id от мёртвого; без него правдоподобный UUID молча превращает починку в её имитацию.
cause: design
open: Настоящий service_id Силли неизвестен коду. Требуется Влад: Railway UI → сервис ai-office-shared → id → SELF_SERVICE_ID (Силли) и SILLI_SERVICE_ID (watchdog-bot). До этого автоподъём лидера не работает — как не работал с 30.05.

title: A hardened parser that lives in shared but was never carried into the caller is not a fix — it is a fix someone else is still missing
symptom: The office group got «⛔ Cilly: баг в villy-bot — команда за 3 попыток не дала код, прошедший ревью», and office:logs showed Девви receiving the same villy-bot task roughly every two minutes for hours. Every attempt failed with the same line: «Рикки не вернул финальный код (блок ```python отсутствует/пуст)». Рикки was returning code the whole time.
root_cause: coder.py extracted the final file with a literal slice: find("```python") to the next "```". It missed «```py» and bare «```» entirely, and because a fence is not nested, any file that itself contains triple backticks got cut at the inner fence and yielded a stub that would not compile. The office already had the correct parser — shared/verify.extract_code, written 01.08.2026 after this exact failure produced three consecutive «unterminated triple-quoted string» attempts. It takes several candidates (outermost slice, longest block) and prefers the one that compiles. It was never carried into coder.py, where the naive slice survived in two places. A second defect compounded it: a worker answer beginning «ERROR: …» means the worker itself could not get the code past verification, and deliberately carries no code — the pipeline answered that with «you forgot the fence», so all three retries told Рикки to fix the wrong thing.
why_architecture: Shared modules make the fixed version available; they do not make it used. Nothing failed when coder.py kept its own copy — the copy worked for the common case, so nobody noticed it was the pre-fix version. The retry loop then hid the cost: a deterministic parse miss looks exactly like a flaky model, and three automatic attempts plus periodic re-triggering turn one wrong regex into hours of paid work and a false escalation to the owner.
fix: Both call sites now go through extract_ricky_code(), a thin wrapper over shared extract_code that additionally treats an «ERROR:» answer as 'no code' rather than something to parse. ricky_failure_reason() replaces the hardcoded diagnosis: an empty answer, a worker refusal (quoted verbatim, with its compiler error) and a genuinely fence-less answer are now three different messages, so the retry feedback tells the worker what actually went wrong. Tests cover ```py, bare fences, a file containing triple quotes (asserting the old slice produces a SyntaxError and the new one compiles), worker errors, and a gate asserting no third copy of the naive slice appears.
prevention: When you harden a parser, grep for the pattern you just replaced across every caller before closing the task — the duplicate you leave behind is the one that will fail, and it will fail looking like a model problem, not a parsing problem. And never let an automated retry invent the reason for a failure: if the far side reported why it failed, quote it; if it said nothing, say that. A retry loop fed a wrong diagnosis does not converge, it just spends three times as much confirming it.
cause: design

title: A system that can only dump its logs cannot answer questions about itself — and during an incident, a truncated dump answers nothing at all
symptom: Diagnosing why the dev department had failed six times in a row on villy-bot needed exactly one number: how often Девви was being handed the same task. There was no way to ask. Four consecutive attempts through Силли's /task returned the raw event list, cut off at 3000 characters — no count, no first timestamp, no last, no interval. The ~2-minute cadence had to be counted by eye off the fragment, and the tail was never visible, so 'is the loop still running right now' stayed unanswered.
root_cause: The office had log_event() for writing and read_logs() for reading, and nothing in between. Every question about logs went through the agentic loop, which reads a Redis key and echoes it; the reply path then truncates at 3000 chars. So the answer to 'how many' was a prefix of the data, and the answer to 'when did it stop' was structurally unavailable — the tail is exactly what truncation removes. Instructing the model to 'answer with one line, no dumps' did not help: it complied with the retrieval and ignored the formatting, four times.
why_architecture: Aggregation has to happen before the transport limit, not after. Any observability path that ships raw records through a bounded channel degrades to 'a prefix of the truth' precisely when volume is high — and high volume IS the incident signal. The office also has two populations of log writers: the 15 bots in identity.BOTS, and the dev-department workers (девви, рикки, тести, секки, скрибби) which are not in the registry at all. Anything that enumerates 'all bots' from the registry silently omits the five that mattered here.
fix: shared/log_query.py: summarize() returns total, first/last timestamp, span, per-event and per-level counts, and the MEDIAN interval between consecutive occurrences of the dominant event — median rather than mean so one long pause does not mask a steady beat. discover_bots() enumerates writers by scanning Redis keys instead of trusting the registry. GET /logs on Силли exposes it with bot/days/event/level/limit/format; the summary is always present and entries are opt-in (limit defaults to 0), so the answer to 'what is happening' is one line rather than a truncated list. Documented in SYSTEM_STATE next to the office:logs key contract.
prevention: Give every store of operational data a query path that returns aggregates, not just a dump — and build it before the incident, because during one you will reach for whatever exists. When a channel truncates, aggregate on the far side of the truncation. And when enumerating 'everything of a kind', derive the list from the data (which keys exist) rather than from a registry (which names we remembered to add): the entries missing from the registry are disproportionately the ones nobody is watching.
cause: gap

title: Wiring that provably delivers can still deliver the wrong thing: the banter fanout worked end-to-end while sending every bot the human's line and none of the answers
symptom: Both banter waves fired cleanly on 16.08 — four bursts, zero failed pings, every skip reason logged. The output still did not read as a conversation: the invited bots all answered Влад rather than each other, two bots in the same wave said the same thing in different words, replies arrived cut mid-word, and Милли answered a line addressed to Билли as if Билли were her name.
root_cause: Every one of those defects lived in the same 3 lines that built `message`: the prompt was `BANTER_PROMPT + «Последним говорил: X» + trigger_text[:200]`. trigger_text is the HUMAN's message, so the answer the primary agent had just posted — the thing worth reacting to — was never shown. The string was built once before the loop, so the second bot in a wave physically could not obey «не повторяй уже сказанное»: it saw exactly what the first one saw. `[:200]` is a byte slice, so a reply ended «...деплой упа». And nothing in the prompt distinguished the addressee of a remark from its recipient, although in banter they are almost never the same bot — the whole point is that we ping a third party.
why_architecture: Delivery telemetry and output quality are different questions, and the telemetry answered loudly enough to look like an answer to both. `banter_ping agents=... failed=нет` proves the HTTP hop; it says nothing about what was in the payload, so a fully instrumented, fully green feature produced unusable text for days. The context the feature needed already existed in `office:group:history` — written by Филли for the human and by every bot for itself, specifically so that bots could see who said what — but banter never read it and carried its own impoverished substitute instead. Same shape as lesson #100: the good version exists in shared and the caller keeps its own.
fix: The prompt is now assembled per recipient from a transcript: _chat_tail() reads office:group:history, in-wave replies are appended as they arrive so each subsequent bot sees its colleagues, and build_message() renders «Кто: что» with the last speaker named. clip() cuts on a word boundary and collapses newlines, replacing both [:200] slices. BANTER_RULES spells out the rules that «одна короткая реплика» did not cover, including «реплика адресована не тебе — не отвечай за адресата». strip_self_prefix() drops a model's own signature so the second wave does not quote «Милли: Милли: ...». A one-word reply no longer seeds a second wave. context_lines threads wave 1 into wave 2 so the second wave does not depend on the recipient having written itself to the ленту before answering. BANTER_COOLDOWN (SET NX + TTL, 60s) caps burst frequency. 27 tests in tests/test_banter_quality.py.
prevention: When a feature's output is text a model writes, review the exact string that goes into the prompt — print one and read it — before concluding from green telemetry that the feature works. «Pinged, 200 OK» and «said something worth reading» are separate claims needing separate evidence. Two specifics that generalise: an instruction the model cannot possibly satisfy («don't repeat what was said» when it was not shown what was said) is worse than no instruction, because it looks like the requirement is covered; and any threshold that decides whether to act («шуметь ли») needs a companion ceiling that remembers whether it just acted («не шумели ли только что») — the same SET NX + TTL that fixes duplicate alerts.
cause: design

title: Two independent paths answering the same question is not redundancy — it is two answers that can disagree, and the office had both kinds at once
symptom: Two complaints that looked like one: «теперь всё роутит только Гослингу по умолчанию», and «я прям чётко спросил Гослинга с пересланным сообщением, а Филли роутит к Билли». Neither was a routing regression. In the 08:41 window Гослинг answered a single «С добрым утром» TWICE — a one-liner at 08:42:01 and a half-screen monologue at 08:42:06.
